summary: The toll-keepers by Benjamin Clarke is a collection of short stories for children written in the late 19th century. Blending homely vignettes, maritime anecdotes, travel sketches, and gentle moral lessons, it likely centers on everyday kindness, courage, and faith, using lively incidents to instruct and entertain young readers. Across the volume, brief tales range from the tender title piece—two little farm girls “keeping toll” at their gate while awaiting their father—to brisk sea-yarns and travel notes. “Chips” offers true naval anecdotes (a monkey scattering a hoard and a Kadi’s wry justice; foes later meeting as friends), while lively sketches recount Gibraltar’s strength and Malta’s curiosities (including the eerie Capuchin catacombs). Domestic and devotional portraits—of a steadfast grandson’s love, a moving visit to the children’s hospital, and a providential dream that unmasks a plot—underscore the book’s themes of compassion, self-control, industry, and trust in God.
